name: Driftwood
title: The product was working. The website was losing the room.
tagline: Repositioning and rebuilding the site for an AI sales agent — researched, coded, and shipped in 18 hours.

heroMedia.alt: The new driftwood.sh homepage — 'Ship a custom demo in every cold message' beside the live product dashboard

intro: Driftwood is an AI sales agent for demo-led outbound: it researches each prospect, builds them a working custom demo, and sends it from the founder's own account. A genuinely different product — with a website that made it sound like everything else.
The founder had run 20+ sales conversations and landed one client. The problem wasn't the product. It was a single misconception the site never corrected.

sections.label: The misconception
sections.heading: People thought the demo was a one-time thing
body: Prospects who saw the old site assumed Driftwood generated one generic demo of your product and blasted it out. That reading made it just another AI outbound tool — easy to dismiss in a market drowning in AI slop.
The reality is the opposite: Driftwood builds a new custom demo, tailored to every single client it contacts. That's the whole value. And it was the one thing visitors consistently didn't take away.

sections.label: Words before pixels
sections.heading: We tested the story on real prospects before touching the design
body: Instead of redesigning on instinct, we took new language and framing into in-person conversations with potential clients and watched where understanding clicked — and where it broke.

Once the framing corrected the misconception, the founder landed three more clients — before a single pixel of the new site existed. That was the green light: the message was validated with revenue, and the site's only job was to deliver it.

media.alt: Side-by-side on the new site: the generic AI-written cold email everyone else sends, versus the researched, demo-backed message Driftwood sent
media.caption: The reframe, made visible: what everyone else sends vs. what Driftwood sent — same leads, 14× the replies in week one at Autosana.

sections.label: The pivotal moment
sections.heading: Show the moment the product becomes obvious
body: Every explanation of Driftwood eventually hits one pivotal beat: the agent has already researched the prospect and built them their own working demo. Text kept burying that moment, so I built it as motion — you watch the demo get made for a specific company, not described in the abstract.
It's the first thing you understand on the new homepage, before you've read a paragraph.

media.alt: The new driftwood.sh homepage, scrolling from the hero through the product story
media.caption: The shipped homepage. The hero shows the outcome; the pivotal moment plays out on screen instead of being explained.

sections.label: Architecture
sections.heading: An information architecture that sells
body: The old page order answered the founder's questions, not the prospect's. I rebuilt the IA around the objections people actually raised in the test conversations, in the order they raised them: what is this → is it slop → prove it's custom → show me the product → let me book.
Each section earns the next scroll. Nothing on the page exists because it 'should be there' — it exists because a real prospect needed it to say yes.

sections.label: Proof
sections.heading: Case studies you can skim — that still feel special
body: The degree of customization is Driftwood's proof, so I designed a case study section that shows it: real demos the agent built for real companies, presented so a visitor gets the point in seconds but can go as deep as they want.
Skimmable was the constraint. If a prospect has to read to feel the customization, the section has failed — the visual variety of the demos does the arguing.

media.alt: Scrolling through the case studies section — each card a different custom demo Driftwood built
media.caption: Every card is a different demo the agent built. The variety is the argument.

sections.label: The dashboard
sections.heading: The dashboard section, without the essay
body: The old 'explore the dashboard' section was word-heavy, with screenshots that had no visual focus — visitors couldn't distill the value quickly, so they skipped it.

I replaced it with an interactive, highlightable dashboard: hover a feature and it lights up with a one-line explanation. Same information, but you explore it instead of reading it. The section went from the most-skipped part of the page to the part that shows the product actually working.

media.alt: The interactive dashboard section — hovering different regions highlights each feature with a short caption
media.caption: Hover to highlight. Each region of the real dashboard explains itself in one line.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.heading: Positioning is a design deliverable
body: The highest-leverage design work on this project happened before any interface existed: finding the one sentence prospects were getting wrong and fixing it in conversation, with evidence. The website is that sentence, made visual and shipped.
Given 18 hours end-to-end — meetings included — I coded and shipped it myself. It's live at driftwood.sh.
